title: 3 ways marketing automation platforms are being reinvented
content:
For most of the last 20 years, marketing automation platforms helped B2B marketers answer one central question: Is this lead ready for sales?
Marketo, Eloqua, Pardot, and similar platforms gave marketers a database, behavioral tracking, segmentation, scoring, workflows, email, and CRM integration. Marketing could collect signals about prospects, interpret those signals, and automate the action.
At the time, this model made sense for the information marketers had available.
You tracked someone’s behavioral activity. You’d know if they downloaded a white paper, attended a webinar, visited the pricing page, or opened three emails.
Marketing used those activities as signals of interest. Lead scoring helped us qualify them, and nurture programs helped us move people along. Eventually, someone crossed a threshold and went to sales for follow-up.
Much of the marketing operations function developed around making that machinery work. That model is now being reinvented along three different paths.
Salesforce and Adobe are building marketing orchestration on top of much broader customer data environments. Braze organizes automation around customer behavior and engagement across the lifecycle. Inflection.io is making a different bet and rebuilding the traditional marketing automation platform around modern customer data and buying behavior.
These three approaches point toward a larger question for the MAP category: What decision should a marketing automation platform help marketing make?
Underneath all those smart campaigns, engagement programs, and scoring models, traditional marketing automation always contained a basic decision engine. Think of it as three layers: Data → Decision → Action.
Those systems were doing what we now call decisioning. They simply had fewer inputs and fewer possible actions. The objective was fairly simple: to qualify demand and move it toward sales.
The current data environment surrounding these platforms is considerably broader. Marketing can potentially know about product usage, purchases, service interactions, account activity, mobile behavior, subscriptions, transactions, sales conversations, and activity across an entire buying group all in a single location.
Sales readiness is still important, but now it’s one possible customer state among many. This evolution is shaping the future of MAPs. The question is which approach will win.
The world’s most powerful SEO platform, purpose-built for Enterprise.
Salesforce and Adobe offer a glimpse of where marketing automation could be headed.
Marketing Cloud Next is Salesforce’s agentic marketing solution. It sits on Salesforce’s broader platform, with Data 360 providing customer data that marketers can use for segmentation, personalization, and orchestration. Flow Builder can then coordinate journeys and actions using that information.
Adobe follows a similar direction. Adobe Journey Optimizer uses Adobe Experience Platform data to build dynamic journeys that can respond to engagement and business events across acquisition, upsell, cross-sell, and retention. Marketo Engage continues to provide marketing automation capabilities within the larger Adobe ecosystem.
Essentially, we start with the unified customer record. Then put decisioning, journey orchestration, and execution capabilities on top of it. The center of gravity is the customer data infrastructure.
Marketing automation becomes one application of that infrastructure alongside sales, service, commerce, etc.
This potentially reduces the importance of having a standalone marketing database sitting between your CRM and the rest of the stack.
Braze approaches automation from another direction. It calls itself a customer engagement platform. Its architecture centers on customer profiles, real-time behavioral data, and coordinated engagement across channels.
A MOps team probably isn’t evaluating Braze as a direct Marketo replacement. Its relevance comes from what its architecture tells us about the direction of automation.
Braze represents a next-gen approach to marketing automation that expands how automation works across the customer lifecycle. Its Data Platform connects customer information with its engagement platform so companies can respond to customer behavior and changing context. Journeys can extend through acquisition, onboarding, engagement, adoption, retention, expansion, and win-back.
This puts more responsibility on marketing to manage engagement with this customer based on what they’re doing right now. That shifts the center from the database to the customer lifecycle.
The system follows the customer through acquisition, onboarding, usage, retention, expansion, and re-engagement.
Braze represents a potential expansion of what we mean by marketing automation. The MAP historically helped marketing create and qualify demand. The customer engagement model helps coordinate the relationship over time.
Platform news, strategy analysis, and industry trends. Trusted by 40,000+ marketing professionals.
Inflection.io represents a third direction. Its approach keeps marketing automation as its own platform while updating it for how modern B2B companies operate.
Inflection was originally built around product-led businesses, giving marketers access to product activity and customer behavior that traditional MAPs often struggled to use effectively.
The company later focused on traditional marketing automation. In 2026, Inflection added capabilities for sales-led companies, including Salesforce opportunity synchronization, native forms, speed-to-lead functionality, and account scoring. It now positions itself directly against Marketo and Pardot.
The company’s background makes this approach worth watching. Its founders and leadership include people with experience at Bizible, Marketo, and Adobe.
The model keeps the familiar pieces of a MAP, like forms, email, segmentation, CRM synchronization, and campaigns. Then it adds richer product, account, CRM, and customer data and modernizes the workflows built around them.
The central question becomes what the platform should optimize around. Campaign execution has traditionally occupied that position. Customer context and decisioning could increasingly take its place.
Traditional marketing automation worked roughly like this: Collect signals → Score → Nurture → Qualify → Send to sales.
The emerging model looks more like: Collect customer data → Understand context → Determine the next action → Coordinate the response → Learn from what happens.
The unresolved question is where the intelligence should live.
Salesforce and Adobe are putting customer data under orchestration. Braze organizes decisioning around customer behavior and engagement across the lifecycle. Inflection keeps marketing automation as the primary application and modernizes the data and functionality available within it.
We don’t know which architecture will dominate. We can see the problem they’re all trying to solve.
Marketing has more customer information than it can effectively use. The next generation of marketing automation aims to turn that information into useful decisions.
MOps grew up asking questions like, what score creates an MQL? Which nurture should this person enter? Where should this lead route? Which workflow should fire?
The next layer of questions gets closer to customer decisioning.
MOps increasingly has to translate customer behavior into business rules and outcomes. The goal is to understand how your marketing automation architecture will work when decisions rely on customer context rather than a handful of marketing interactions.
Marketers have spent decades asking for a 360-degree view of the customer. We’re getting closer.
The next challenge is making that information useful. A customer profile containing hundreds of attributes, behaviors, and interactions only helps when marketing knows which signals matter and what should happen because of them.
